title: Mental practice for arm recovery early after stroke
official: MEntal practice for the RehabIliTation of the upper-limb in acute Stroke: a feasibility randomised controlled trial with process evaluation
summary:
Background and study aims
In the UK, over 100,000 people experience a stroke every year. After stroke, up to 70% of people experience problems using their shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand (upper limb) to undertake even simple daily tasks, reducing independence and well-being. UK stroke clinical guidelines recommend up to 6 hours of therapeutic activities should be undertaken each day, more than doubling the current best rehabilitation provision in the NHS. This highlights an urgent need to find effective treatments that people after stroke can use independently to augment their rehabilitation.
Mental practice is a promising treatment in which participants listen to a script that facilitates them imagining moving their upper limb to complete a task (e.g., writing). Because mental practice requires no physical movement, it is practical and safe for people with even severe upper-limb limitations to use independently. Systematic reviews indicate that mental practice improves upper-limb function, but few trials have evaluated mental practice in the first weeks after stroke, despite this being when there is the greatest potential for recovery.
Whilst a randomised controlled trial of the effectiveness of mental practice is clearly needed, crucial data on feasibility and acceptability are needed to support its design.
This study aims to explore the feasibility and acceptability of a randomised controlled trial to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of mental practice for the upper limb when delivered in addition to usual rehabilitation and the acceptability of a mental-practice intervention for the upper limb for people between 1 day and 3 months after stroke.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years and over within 4 weeks of their stroke who are currently inpatients and meet the eligibility criteria.

What does the study involve?
Patients will be randomly allocated to either mental practice or relaxation. Both groups will be asked to use the digital application on a tablet computer (which will be loaned to them) for 20 minutes a day, for 5 days a week, over 6 weeks. The digital application involves motor imagery, or relaxation instructions; therefore, there are no physical risks for patients participating. This will be in addition to the standard rehabilitation services currently offered by the patients' admitting NHS hospital.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no major risks associated with participating. Although it has not been reported in other studies, there is a theoretical risk that some participants may be distressed by imagining movements that they cannot physically perform.

Where is the study run from?
The study will be co-ordinated from the Lancashire Clinical Trials Unit based at the University of Lancashire (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to October 2027

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research as part of their Research for Patient Benefit programme (UK)

Who is the main contact?
LCTUMerits@lancashire.ac.uk

interventions.name: Potential research participants will be screened when they attend the stroke wards at the two NHS locations participating in the study. If they are deemed initially eligible, they will be approached and provided with a participant information sheet in both standard text and also an easy-read version

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. At least 18 years old
2. Diagnosed with an ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke within the previous 4 weeks (2 weeks where possible)
3. Demonstrate upper-limb deficits (defined as a National Institute of Health Stroke Scale, NIHSS, Motor Arm score of 1-4 on admission)
4. Baseline Action Research Arm Test of less than 50, indicating significant arm and hand dysfunction
5. Are eligible to receive onward physical rehabilitation either in the community or another rehabilitation setting 
6. Can comprehend simple verbal instructions assessed by Oxford Cognitive Screen and 4 items from a subset of the COMPASS Assessment to assess ability to complete multiple-step instructions 
7. Can provide feedback on experiences (with support from a carer if required)
8. Are likely to be able to undertake mental practice, evidenced by a score indicating more than 50% correctness on hand laterality judgement test (5/10)
Exclusion criteria:
1. Patients who do not have capacity to consent despite materials being available in accessible formats and other languages     
2. Have significant hearing loss despite corrective aids
3. Are not fluent (listening) in English, Polish, Indian Punjabi or Urdu 
4. Receiving end-of-life care
5. Have significant other impairment of the upper limb such as frozen shoulder, complex regional pain syndrome, orthopaedic injury that would prevent completion of movements required for the outcome measurements
6. Have health conditions that limit or prevent engagement with rehabilitation 
7. Currently participating in another stroke rehabilitation trial 
8. Are likely to be discharged to a location outside a practical working distance from the recruitment location during the intervention or follow-up period
